title: Asana — steady and comfortable (2.46–2.48)
hook: the most famous part of yoga gets three short sutras, and the first one is just three words: a seat, steady and comfortable

segments.voice: Yesterday: anuttama. Santosha, the happiness at the end of wanting. Did 'I'll be happy when' turn into 'right now,' even once? Day four hundred sixty-two, the end of a week.

Search the word yoga on any phone and count the bodies. Legs behind heads. Handstands on paddleboards. Whole books of poses, hundreds of them, with names like crow and pigeon and downward dog. Now open the Yoga Sutras, the classic text behind the word, and look for the poses. You'll find the third limb, asana, in sutra 2.46. It's three words long in Sanskrit. Then two more short sutras. Then Patanjali moves on to the breath. That's the whole section.
screen: `HUNDREDS OF POSES ONLINE.` → `OPEN THE YOGA SUTRAS.` → `THREE SHORT SUTRAS.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.46: sthira sukham asanam. Sthira, steady. Sukha, easy, comfortable. Asana, seat. The word comes from a root meaning to sit. It's the seat you meditate in. Steady and comfortable, both at once. Not rigid. Not slumped. Sutra 2.47 says how: by relaxing effort, and letting the mind rest in the endless. Some commentators hear in that word Ananta, the great serpent who holds up the earth without strain. Sutra 2.48 gives the result: then you're not knocked about by the pairs, heat and cold, comfort and discomfort. That's all it says. The classical commentary adds a few names of seats, the lotus, the hero's seat and others, but no instructions, no sequence. The long lists of postures belong to later hatha yoga texts and to modern teachers. None of that makes the postures wrong. It just tells you what Patanjali was after: a body quiet enough to forget, so the inner limbs can begin. Now look back over the week. Aviplava, steady seeing. Ashtanga, from others inward. Yama, ahimsa first. Niyama, the second five. Grounded in non-harm, hostility ceases. Contentment, nothing higher. And today, a seat. A week of the outer limbs, and almost none of it was about the body. Most of it was about how you treat people, including yourself.
screen: `STHIRA, SUKHA: STEADY, EASY.` · `RELAX THE EFFORT.` · `NO LONGER KNOCKED BY THE PAIRS.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `THAT'S ALL IT SAYS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is the whole of 2.46. Find a seat, chair, cushion or floor. First, steady: let the spine rise a little, the base settle down. Then easy: drop the shoulders, unclench the jaw, soften the hands. If something strains, adjust it. Then relax the effort of holding the pose at all, and let the body be held by whatever's under it. When an itch or ache asks for attention, notice it like weather. Steady. Easy. The bell holds the time.
Asana. The seat, the third limb of yoga, which Patanjali describes in three words: steady and comfortable.
Your line: that's all it says. Today, wherever you sit, a desk, a bus, a waiting room, check once: steady? easy? Adjust until both are true. Day four hundred sixty-two.

screen: `DAY 462 COUNTS.` → `A WEEK OF THE OUTER LIMBS, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: PRANAYAMA.`

howItsDone: In the Yoga Sutras, asana is the seated posture for meditation, steady and easy; Hindus who meditate or do japa often sit cross-legged on a mat or cushion, while modern posture classes draw on later hatha yoga traditions.

asana comes from a root meaning to sit
2.47 says the seat is mastered by relaxing effort
and by letting the mind rest in the endless.

fork.setup: your meditation seat is perfectly straight but your whole body is clenched. what would 2.46 say?
options: good: steadiness is all that matters.
it needs to be easy too, steady and comfortable at once.
skip the seat and lie down instead.
fork.reveal: sthira sukham asanam: steady and comfortable, both. 2.47 adds: by relaxing effort.

original.note: Sanskrit āsana: seat, from the root ās, to sit; in 2.46, sthira-sukham āsanam.

trapdoor: what you thought: asana means a yoga pose.
what it means: a seat for meditation, steady and easy, so the body stops calling for attention.
what a scholar hears: three sutras only (2.46–2.48); the commentary names a few seats; posture catalogs come from later hatha texts and modern developments.
